about: Crop list for Field Shift. Edit this file to add a crop or fix a value; the site reads it when it opens. D = water need index (mm), need = frost-free days needed, soil/income/feed = 0-100 indices, heat = suffers in a hot July, carry = mm of soil water left for (or taken from) the next crop. cal = the field through the year, Jan to Dec: P = same as last year's December, B = bare soil, C = crop growing, S = stubble or residue. gaez = FAO GAEZ suitability rating for each area, filled in by the team (null = not checked yet). All numbers are rough estimates for a local agronomist to check.

wheat.name: Spring wheat
wheat.role: Wheat is the main crop of the belt, with the most reliable market.
wheat.why: Wheat stays in the plan because farms have the equipment and buyers for it.
benefits: Familiar equipment, seed and grain markets.
Stubble left standing protects the soil over winter.
checks: Wheat after wheat builds up root diseases and weeds.

barley.name: Spring barley
barley.role: Barley ripens early and leaves stubble that protects the soil through the windy spring.
barley.why: Barley matures earlier than wheat, which helps where the frost-free season is short.
benefits: Stubble traps snow and protects against wind erosion.
Uses the same seeding and harvest equipment as wheat.
Grain can be sold or fed to animals.
checks: Cereal after cereal can build up root diseases and grassy weeds.
Check barley demand (feed or malting) locally.

oats.name: Oats (grain)
oats.role: Oats cope with cool weather and poorer soil, and the grain feeds animals well.
oats.why: Oats are a cereal that does not carry the main wheat root diseases.
benefits: A partial break from wheat diseases.
Grain and straw are both useful feed.
Same equipment as wheat.
checks: Lower market price than wheat.
Oats suffer in hot, dry spells at grain filling.

millet.name: Proso millet
millet.role: Millet needs very little water and a short season, but frost kills it.
millet.why: Millet is sown late and ripens fast, so it can follow a failed or late-sown crop.
benefits: Among the lowest water needs of any grain.
Likes heat that hurts other crops.
Short season of about 70 to 90 days.
checks: Any frost kills it, so sowing waits until June.
Seed drops easily at harvest.
The local market may be small.

buckwheat.name: Buckwheat
buckwheat.role: Buckwheat grows fast in a short season and smothers weeds, but even a light frost kills it.
buckwheat.why: Buckwheat is sown late and is ready in about 70 to 80 days.
benefits: Very short season.
Shades out weeds.
A food crop with its own market, different from wheat.
checks: Killed by even a light frost at both ends of the season.
Flowers can fail in hot, dry spells.
Check whether there is a buyer nearby.

pea.name: Field pea
pea.role: Peas feed the soil with nitrogen and give a crop to sell or feed in place of a rest year.
pea.why: Peas take nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil for the next wheat crop.
benefits: Adds nitrogen, so the following wheat may need less fertilizer.
Breaks wheat root-disease and weed cycles.
Peas can be sold or used as protein feed.
checks: Check for a reliable local buyer.
Pea residue is light: check how well it protects soil in spring.
Sensitive to heat during flowering in July.

lentil.name: Lentil
lentil.role: Lentils feed the soil with nitrogen and use very little water.
lentil.why: Lentils fix nitrogen like peas and suit drier fields.
benefits: Adds nitrogen for the next wheat crop.
Very low water need.
A food crop with good value for its weight.
checks: Short plants are hard to harvest without the right equipment.
Sensitive to heat at flowering.
Light residue: check spring soil cover.

chickpea.name: Chickpea
chickpea.role: Chickpeas handle heat and drought well and sell for a good price, but need a long season.
chickpea.why: Chickpeas are a nitrogen-fixing crop for hot, dry fields.
benefits: Adds nitrogen to the soil.
Deep roots cope with dry spells.
Higher value than most grains.
checks: Needs one of the longer frost-free seasons here and ripens slowly in a cool, wet autumn.
Little local experience: try a small area first.
Leaf diseases spread in wet weather.

rape.name: Rapeseed
rape.role: Rapeseed is a cash crop that breaks wheat diseases, but needs a longer season and more water.
rape.why: Rapeseed is a non-cereal break crop with a deep taproot and a growing market.
benefits: Breaks cereal disease cycles.
Taproot can open up compacted soil.
Higher market value than cereals.
checks: Sensitive to heat at flowering.
High water need in dry summers.
Flea beetles and seed costs need local advice.

mustard.name: Mustard
mustard.role: Mustard's deep taproot loosens hard soil, and it needs less water than rapeseed.
mustard.why: Mustard is a short-season break crop that Mongolian conservation farmers have used in rotations.
benefits: Taproot loosens hard soil layers.
Short season and modest water need.
Breaks cereal disease cycles.
checks: The market for mustard seed may be small.
Flea beetles can damage young plants.
Heat at flowering lowers seed set.

flax.name: Flax (linseed)
flax.role: Flax suits cool summers and uses little water, but competes poorly with weeds.
flax.why: Flax is a non-cereal break crop that uses less water than rapeseed.
benefits: Breaks wheat disease cycles.
Lower water need than most cash crops.
Linseed is traded internationally.
checks: Flax leaves thin residue, so spring soil cover is weaker than it looks here.
Competes poorly with weeds.
Check buyers and price locally.

sunflower.name: Sunflower
sunflower.role: Sunflower has a good market but needs a long season, so early frost is a real risk here.
sunflower.why: Sunflower is a deep-rooted oilseed, shown so farmers can see the risk of a long-season crop.
benefits: Deep roots reach water other crops cannot.
Oilseed with steady demand.
Breaks cereal disease cycles.
checks: Needs the longest frost-free season of any crop here.
Deep roots leave the soil dry for the next crop.
Wide rows leave soil open in early summer.

oathay.name: Oats for hay
oathay.role: Oats cut green for hay need the shortest season and give winter feed for livestock.
oathay.why: Hay oats are cut in August, before frost matters, and herders need winter fodder.
benefits: Short season: lower frost risk than grain crops.
Hay for your own animals or for sale to herders.
Stubble and regrowth cover the soil into winter.
checks: Hay price and demand change from year to year.
Removing hay takes nutrients off the field.
June sowing leaves soil bare for a few weeks in early summer.

vetchoat.name: Vetch and oat hay mix
vetchoat.role: Vetch sown with oats makes richer hay than oats alone and adds nitrogen to the soil.
vetchoat.why: The vetch fixes nitrogen while the oats hold it up, giving protein-rich hay in a short season.
benefits: Higher-protein hay than oats alone.
Vetch adds nitrogen for the next crop.
Cut in August, so frost risk is low.
checks: Vetch seed can be costly or hard to find.
Removing hay takes nutrients off the field.
Check the right seed mix with a local agronomist.

alfalfa.name: Alfalfa
alfalfa.role: Alfalfa stays in the ground for years, covers the soil, builds it and gives the best hay, but uses a lot of water.
alfalfa.why: Alfalfa is a deep-rooted perennial legume that keeps the soil covered all year once established.
benefits: The best soil builder here: nitrogen, organic matter and deep roots.
Soil stays covered once it is established.
High-quality hay for winter feed or sale.
checks: Uses a lot of water and leaves the soil dry for the next crop.
Needs hardy varieties to survive Mongolian winters.
Real stands are often kept three to five years.

maize.name: Silage maize
maize.bare: Silage harvest takes the whole plant, so the soil is left bare.
maize.role: Maize cut green for silage gives a lot of feed, but needs warmth, water and a long season.
maize.why: Silage maize produces more feed per hectare than hay crops where the season allows.
benefits: Very high feed yield in a good year.
Silage keeps well for winter.
Breaks wheat disease cycles.
checks: Frost kills it, and it needs a long, warm season.
Harvest leaves the soil bare through winter and spring.
Needs silage equipment and storage.

potato.name: Potato
potato.bare: Digging the potatoes disturbs the whole topsoil and leaves it loose and bare.
potato.role: Potatoes can earn the most, but need a lot of water and leave the soil loose after digging.
potato.why: Potatoes have strong demand in towns and suit farms that can water the field.
benefits: Among the highest earners here.
Breaks cereal disease cycles.
Strong local demand.
checks: Very high water need: realistic mainly with watering.
Digging leaves soil bare and loose through winter and spring.
Frost-sensitive, with storage and labour costs.

carrot.name: Carrots
carrot.bare: Lifting the carrots leaves the soil dug up, loose and bare.
carrot.role: Carrots earn well near towns, but only on fields that can be watered.
carrot.why: Root vegetables turn a farm's water into high value where there is a town market.
benefits: High income with a nearby market.
Breaks cereal disease cycles.
Stores well over winter.
checks: Needs watering, labour and storage.
Harvest leaves soil bare and loose through winter.
Prices change a lot: check buyers before planting.

fallow.name: Bare rest year
fallow.role: A bare rest year saves water, but the soil sits open and can blow away in spring.
fallow.why: The field is cultivated to kill weeds and store moisture for the next wheat crop.
benefits: Stores moisture for the wheat that follows.
Simple weed control through cultivation.
checks: How much topsoil is lost to wind during bare springs on this field.
No income in the rest year.

nofallow.name: Stubble rest year
nofallow.word: a rest year with stubble left standing
nofallow.role: A rest year with the old stubble left standing saves water and keeps the soil covered.
nofallow.why: Weeds are controlled without tillage, so the soil is never left bare.
benefits: Stores more moisture than a bare rest year, because stubble traps snow.
Soil is covered all year, so wind erosion risk is much lower.
checks: Needs a no-till seeder and herbicide weed control.
No income in the rest year.

featured.sum: The usual plan in the wheat belt. The rest year saves water, but the soil sits bare and can blow away in spring.
why: This is common practice in the wheat belt and the reference point for every other plan.
The bare rest year stores soil moisture and controls weeds before the next wheat crop.
benefits: Familiar equipment, seed and grain markets.
The rest year stores moisture for the wheat that follows, which helps in dry years.
Simple weed control through cultivation.
unknowns: How much moisture the rest year really stores on this farm's soil.
How much topsoil is lost to wind during bare springs on this field.

featured.sum: Keeps the rest year to save water, but leaves the old stubble standing so the soil stays covered.
why: Keeps the rest year (moisture storage) but leaves stubble standing instead of cultivating.
Weeds are controlled without tillage, so the soil is never left bare.
benefits: Stores more moisture than a bare rest year (stubble traps snow, less evaporation).
Soil covered all year: much lower wind-erosion risk.
Builds organic matter over time.
unknowns: Needs a no-till seeder and herbicide weed control; cost and access vary.
Weed resistance and herbicide rules need local advice.
Still no crop income in the rest year.

featured.sum: Peas feed the soil with nitrogen and replace the bare rest year with a crop you can sell.
why: Peas take nitrogen from the air, adding soil nitrogen for the next wheat crop.
They replace the bare rest year with a living crop, breaking cereal disease cycles.
benefits: Adds nitrogen, so the following wheat may need less fertilizer.
Breaks wheat root-disease and weed cycles.
A crop to sell in the year that would otherwise earn nothing.
unknowns: Whether there is a reliable local buyer for peas.
Pea residue is light: check how well it protects soil in spring.
Peas are sensitive to heat during flowering in July.

featured.sum: Oats are cut for hay in August. They need the shortest season and give winter feed for livestock.
why: Hay oats are cut in August, so they need the shortest frost-free window.
Herders need winter fodder, so this links crop farms with livestock.
benefits: Short season: lower frost risk than grain crops.
Hay for winter livestock feed or sale to herders.
Stubble and regrowth cover the soil into winter.
unknowns: Hay price and demand vary from year to year and by distance to herders.
Removing hay takes nutrients off the field.
June sowing leaves soil bare for a few weeks in early summer.

featured.sum: A five-year plan: peas between the wheat years, then two years of alfalfa to rebuild the soil and grow hay.
why: Two legumes, peas and alfalfa, add nitrogen and break wheat disease cycles.
Alfalfa keeps the soil covered all year once established and gives hay for livestock.
benefits: Strong soil building from deep alfalfa roots and nitrogen fixing.
Soil is covered through the windy season in the alfalfa years.
Grain, peas and hay spread the risk across three products.
unknowns: Alfalfa uses a lot of water and leaves the soil dry for the wheat that follows.
Needs hardy alfalfa varieties to survive Mongolian winters.
A five-year plan needs steady buyers for peas and hay.
